title: Scientists Burned Their Own Scrolls to Read Ancient Ones
summary:
What would you do to solve a 2,000-year-old mystery? One scientist burned his own scrolls — on purpose!

Here's the story. In 79 C.E., Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman city of Herculaneum. A library of over 1,000 papyrus scrolls was turned into charred, fragile lumps. They're the only intact library from ancient times. But opening them would turn them to dust.

So Douglas Seiler had an idea. He got papyrus and ink from Egypt and Japan. He paid high school students to write on them with passages from Star Wars and the Bible. Then he burned them. Why? To test if lead in the ink could be seen with X-rays.

It worked! Lead absorbs X-rays up to 25 times better than burned papyrus. So writing with lead ink shows up clearly on X-ray CT scans. A cheap handheld scanner can even find lead in a scroll without opening it.

This could help researchers read the Herculaneum scrolls virtually. "The value in this project is practically unquantifiable," said one expert. These scrolls might contain lost works of ancient philosophy. Talk about a hot read!
why_it_matters: It shows how a clever test — even one that means burning things on purpose — can unlock lost knowledge from history, like a library you thought was gone forever.

background_read: Mount Vesuvius (a volcano in Italy) erupted in 79 C.E. and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under hot ash and rock.
The library found at Herculaneum is the only whole ancient library that survived from Roman times — over 1,000 scrolls, all turned into black, burned lumps.
Douglas Seiler (a scientist who wanted a safe way to read burned scrolls) used papyrus from Egypt and ink from Japan for his experiment.
Papyrus is a paper-like material made from a reed plant in Egypt, and it was one of the main things ancient people wrote on.
Article_Structure: WHO: Douglas Seiler, a scientist, plus high school students he paid to write on test scrolls, and experts studying the Herculaneum scrolls.
WHAT: Seiler made his own papyrus scrolls, burned them, and showed that lead in ink can be spotted with X-ray scans — even without opening a scroll.
WHERE: The ancient scrolls come from Herculaneum, a Roman city buried by Mount Vesuvius; the test scrolls used papyrus and ink from Egypt and Japan.
WHY: Opening the real scrolls would turn them to dust, so this trick could let researchers read lost works of ancient philosophy without touching them.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled because the scrolls may hold famous lost books that nobody has read for almost 2,000 years.
They point out that Seiler's test scrolls were new, so real ancient ink and papyrus might behave differently — the method still has to prove itself.
They got paid to copy Star Wars and Bible passages onto scrolls that were then burned, which turned a science test into a fun, strange job.
